narration.text: In his Florentine Diary, Luca Landucci characterises the Venetians as untrustworthy.

caption: Whose judgement does the passage record?

narration.text: We need not accept this description as an objective property of the Venetians. We can instead preserve the act of characterisation itself.

caption: The trait has a conceptual identity.

narration.text: The English expression stays in the passage. Its trait type has an identity of its own. Landucci’s own vocabulary would require the Italian text.
Begin with the Venetians. Other observers might describe them differently. Bringing these characterisations together lets us investigate their reputation.
Begin with the observer, and we can investigate a different history: the language through which that person understood the world.
But we can reverse the direction of inquiry.
Begin with the trait itself, and discover the occasions on which that concept has been applied to the world.

caption: The concept leads back to its textual evidence.

narration.text: Each statement leads back to a passage. Here, researchers have associated two expressions with the same concept: untrustworthy, and not to be trusted.

caption: Concepts have relationships of their own.

narration.text: And the trait type itself can belong to a wider network of concepts, each with its own relationships and history of application.
We can trace the history of things.
We can trace the history of ideas.
And we can trace the history of their meeting.
